skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: Node/Leaf equality and child-offset patterns
skill.trigger: Bug reports about AST/parameter/token parsing that show incorrect booleans for token presence or IndexError when accessing child tokens.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: In parser/front-end libraries, token node types often implement custom equality (e.g., comparing a Leaf to a string by returning self.value == other). This design makes direct equality with strings readable but creates brittle interactions with language-level operations that invoke equality on the other operand (for example tuple membership checks use element == candidate, so a membership test like `node in ('*','**')` will call str.__eq__ and not node.__eq__). Additionally, parser code commonly uses integer offsets into children lists to skip optional tokens (annotations, star markers, commas). Reusable priors:
- Prioritize files/classes named tree.py, node.py, parser/, and classes called Param/Tfpdef/Leaf when parsing/parameter bugs appear.
- Inspect __eq__ / comparison helpers and any code that computes offsets with expressions like `int(self.children[0] in ('*','**'))` or `children[offset]`.
- Expect two confusable code paths: (1) wrong offset (child index off-by-one) causing incorrect default/annotation/star detection; (2) asymmetric equality causing membership/comparison to behave invertedly. Both can coexist.
- When verifying fixes prefer explicit comparisons (e.g., check .value or compare types) or compute offsets using integer checks based on token values using the same side of equality (e.g., compare child.value in set) to avoid relying on reversed __eq__ semantics.
Anti_patterns: assume Node vs str comparisons are symmetric; ignore small helper mixins that override __eq__ and affect membership checks.

skill.title: super().__init__ called but expected base removed or signature changed
skill.trigger: TypeError at instantiation mentioning object.__init__ or unexpected args; presence of unconditional super().__init__ in a class whose bases may have changed.
skill.knowledge:
Fault mode: calling superclass initializer under an assumed base-class contract that no longer holds.
- Mechanism: A derived class invokes super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) expecting a non-trivial base-class initializer (e.g., ErrorFinder.__init__) to accept those arguments. If the derived class no longer inherits that base (or the base's signature was changed/removed), Python resolves super() to object.__init__ (or another unexpected initializer) which rejects extra arguments and raises TypeError at construction time.
- Evidence signals: TypeError message referencing object.__init__; class header showing removed/changed base; unconditional super().__init__ usage; related recent diffs touching class definition or imports of the base.
- Root-location bias: inspect the class header and its __init__ before chasing downstream symptom reporters; check recent commits that altered inheritance or imports.
- Confusable alternatives: wrapper-forwarding mistakes (missing attribute initialization) or changed argument semantics; confirm by inspecting base-class definition and call sites.
- Fix preference: restore the base-class inheritance or change the derived __init__ to avoid forwarding unsupported args (e.g., call super().__init__ only when the expected base is present, adapt arguments, or explicitly initialize required state).

edit_history.rationale: There is no existing fault-mode skill that explicitly describes the 'super().__init__ called while base removed/changed -> object.__init__ TypeError' pattern. This is a clear, transferable causal mechanism worth capturing as its own fault_mode skill.
evidence: Runtime symptom: TypeError: object.__init__() takes exactly one argument (the instance to initialize).
Source: parso/python/pep8.py __init__ uses super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) while class header in patch changed from inheriting ErrorFinder to no base.
edit_history.risk: Low to moderate — risk of misapplying to cases where signature changes (not base removal) matter; mitigated by requiring the TypeError and class/header evidence signals.

skill.title: api_wrapper_or_sdk_emulator: Response-handler and dispatch priors for SDK emulators
skill.trigger: Failures where client SDK calls (boto3-style) raise KeyError/ClientError or tests assert missing top-level keys (e.g., 'ApplicationResponse'/'ApplicationsResponse') and the repository has modules named responses.py / urls.py / models for services.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: For repositories that implement an SDK emulator (HTTP handlers that mimic a cloud API), the response handler layer (files named responses.py, urls.py) and the central BaseResponse utilities are the primary fault surface for API-contract regressions.
- Prioritize opening service/response handlers (responses.py) and urls.py when SDK calls fail with missing keys or unexpected JSON shapes. Look for: parsing of incoming JSON (are requests expected nested under a wrapper like CreateXRequest?), construction of returned bodies (are returned dicts wrapped under expected envelope keys like 'XResponse' or 'ApplicationsResponse'?), and whether handlers return raw strings vs (status, headers, body) tuples used by central dispatch.
- Check the project's BaseResponse/type dispatch utilities (common file like moto/core/responses.py) to see how handler return values are normalized (_transform_response/_enrich_response) and whether method_dispatch wrappers are used in urls to route HTTP methods correctly.
- Typical localization signals: (1) tests assert presence of a specific envelope key (e.g., 'ApplicationsResponse'), (2) handler code returns a to_json() without wrapping, (3) request parsing reads fields at the wrong nesting level (should look for wrapper keys like 'CreateApplicationRequest'), (4) urls.py uses direct dispatch instead of method_dispatch wrappers which expect specific handler signatures.
Anti_patterns: searching only for backend/model logic (e.g., App.to_json()) without checking the response layer that wraps/unpacks requests and responses. Assuming tests are wrong—first check response handler contract.

edit_history.rationale: This case reveals a reusable repository-family prior: SDK/emulator projects (like moto) centralize HTTP-to-backend translation in response handler modules and urls dispatch. Creating a project_type skill captures where to look (responses.py, urls.py, models backends, and central BaseResponse helpers) for similar failures across other services.
evidence: moto/pinpoint/responses.py: create_app reads params = json.loads(self.body) then name = params.get('Name') (should parse CreateApplicationRequest wrapper).

moto/pinpoint/responses.py: create/get/delete/get_apps return app.to_json() / resp directly without 'ApplicationResponse' / 'ApplicationsResponse' envelopes; tests expect those envelopes (tests/test_pinpoint.py asserts ApplicationsResponse).

moto/pinpoint/urls.py: url paths should use BaseResponse.method_dispatch wrappers to call instance methods with (request, full_url, headers) and transform return shapes; mismatch here affects dispatch and envelope handling.

moto/core/responses.py: method_dispatch and _enrich_response control how handler returns are normalized into (status, headers, body) and how headers/status are stringified; response-shape bugs often surface here.
edit_history.risk: Low — captures repository-structure prior; may over-prioritize response handlers in rare bugs that are truly in backend model serialization.

Preferred remediation: either reintroduce stable accessor properties or change aggregators to use the canonical backend-dict lookups (e.g., ec2_backends[acct][region]) or a single adapter helper. Confusable alternatives: missing initialization of an instance attribute vs. an intentionally removed API — confirm by reviewing the property definitions and recent commits.

skill.trigger: Mutating API appears to do nothing because target model collections are empty or populated later.
skill.knowledge:
Title: lazy_model_population_missing_side_effects
Trigger: Mutating API appears to do nothing (no side-effects) because it searches in-memory model collections that are populated later or by other API flows.
Knowledge: In SDK-emulator backends, some model objects/collections (e.g., group.instance_states, backend.instances) are created or populated by separate helpers (creation flows, describe endpoints, set_desired_capacity, replace_autoscaling_group_instances). If a mutating call iterates those collections to apply changes, it can silently miss targets when invoked before population. Reusable priors:
- Root-location bias: inspect both the mutating method (where it searches/filters model collections) and the model-population helpers; the bug often lives in the population timing or in the mutator assuming population has occurred.
- Evidence signals: mutator code filters a .instance_states / .instances list; tests call API immediately after create; helpers named replace_*/set_* exist elsewhere; describe_* functions return elements from the same collection.
- Confusable alternatives: wrong ID mapping or membership checks — confirm collection emptiness vs. mismatched IDs before concluding ordering issue.
- Fix preference: either ensure creation/population happens during group creation (eagerly), or make the mutator canonicalize/retrieve targets via a stable accessor that performs on-demand population, or document/validate API ordering (raise if targets not present).

edit_history.rationale: The failure demonstrates a concrete, transferable defect mechanism where emulator models are populated separately from API mutators. This is a distinct fault-mode (not just 'missing initialization') because the collection is filled later by separate helpers and causes silent no-ops; creating a focused fault-mode skill captures this subpattern without muddying existing 'missing init' skills.

Title: inspect_model_population_and_api_call_order

skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: argument-validation lives in small SyntaxRule loops over node.children
skill.trigger: Bug reports where many argument-related syntax errors (repeated keyword args, positional after keyword unpacking, unparenthesized generator expression in calls) are no longer reported in a parser library.
skill.knowledge:
In parser/front-end projects, syntactic validation for constructs like function argument lists is commonly implemented inside small SyntaxRule classes (e.g., arglist/argument rules) that iterate node.children and set small state flags (kw_only, kw_unpacking_only, arg_set). Reusable priors:
- When a user reports multiple related argument-validation failures (repeated keyword args, positional-after-keyword, generator-expression parenthesization), prioritize files named errors.py/grammar/rules and classes/registers like @ErrorFinder.register_rule(type='arglist'|'argument').
- Look for loops over node.children (for argument in node.children) and small state flags; these loops implement many localized checks. If many checks are missing, search for removed/short-circuited loop bodies, early returns, or refactors that replaced iteration with a no-op.
- Confusable alternatives: tokenization/AST shape changes (verify node.children contents) and asymmetric equality bugs. Distinguish by printing node.children (types and .value) first; if children look correct but no issues are added, inspect for missing loop bodies or deleted self.add_issue calls.
- Ranking bias: raise priority of opening SyntaxRule implementations and any recent diffs touching them when an entire class of related syntactic checks disappears.

Also watch for PEP8 normalizer implementations (parso/python/pep8.py, PEP8Normalizer._visit_node) where entire rule bodies may have been removed or replaced with a no-op (e.g., a `pass`) during a refactor; these files are high-priority when many style checks vanish. Also check for incorrect membership/substring tests (e.g., `if typ in 'import_name'`) that silently fail to match the intended node types.
anti_patterns: Assuming missing errors imply tokenization is wrong without first opening SyntaxRule implementations.
Only grepping for error messages; miss the structural loop that produces them.

edit_history.rationale: The case provides a reusable repository-structure lesson about where argument validation lives in parser frontends (SyntaxRule classes iterating node.children). Existing weak parser skills focus on __eq__/child-offset patterns; this is a distinct, actionable pattern (validation implemented by loops over argument nodes that can be accidentally removed). Create a new project_type skill rather than updating an unrelated weak candidate.

skill.knowledge:
Title: start_pos_tuple_index_confusion_and_misordered_error_args

Trigger: Reported error coordinates or message/code fields are wrong (wrong line or column reported, or message/text swapped), especially in parser/normalizer/error-assembly code.

Knowledge: When error reporting is incorrect, inspect the error-assembly site (ErrorFinder.add_issue, error dicts, normalization helpers) for two common mistakes: (1) indexing the start_pos tuple with the wrong element (mixing up start_pos[0] vs start_pos[1] so line/column are swapped); (2) constructing error records with arguments in the wrong order (e.g., storing (message, code, node) instead of (code, message, node)), which changes what callers print. These mistakes often occur near the boundary where node/leaf start positions are consumed to populate an aggregator keyed by line or when building tuples/dicts for later rendering. skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: leaf-level string-payload regex and slicing are a localization hotspot
skill.trigger: Incorrect decoded string contents (extra or missing leading/trailing characters) for escape-sequence examples; consumer code calls a leaf._get_payload() or similar before decoding.
skill.knowledge:
In parser/front-end projects the inner textual payload of string tokens is frequently extracted inside Leaf/tree classes with a small regex and manual slicing. This pattern is a recurring localization hotspot:
- Root-location bias: open tree/leaf modules (e.g., tree.py) and search for methods named _get_payload/get_payload or regexes on Leaf.value. These are high-priority when decoded string content (after escape processing) is wrong.
- Observable signal: a consumer (normalizer/errors) calls leaf._get_payload() or similar then passes the result to codecs.unicode_escape_decode or codecs.escape_decode; tests/reports show wrong content for escape sequences (e.g., 'u"\\x"' -> extra leading char).
- Confusable alternatives: tokenizer producing wrong token.value, or wrong decoder chosen (b vs unicode); confirm by inspecting both token.value and the regex/slicing in the leaf.
- Ranking bias: prioritize leaf-level payload extractor files (tree.py, token wrapper classes) over higher-level normalizers when decoded payloads are incorrect.
Recommended stable rule: prefer inspecting and unit-testing the regex grouping and slicing that compute the payload; ensure group boundaries exclude quotes and prefixes, and add explicit tests for common escape sequences (e.g., '\\x', '\\u', raw vs byte prefixes).

edit_history.rationale: This case demonstrates a reusable project-level pattern: parser frontends commonly implement string payload extraction inside Leaf classes (tree.py) using small regexes and manual slicing. That pattern is distinct from other existing parser skills (which focus on prefix propagation or SyntaxRule loops), so a new project_type skill focused on leaf-level payload extraction is justified.

Fault-mode: When code splits a string into segments and then merges selected adjacent segments using index arithmetic and deletion, it commonly suffers from off-by-one or wrong-direction bugs. Reusable diagnostics and priors:
- Symptom pattern: examples with special separators (form-feed \x0c, vertical-tab \x0b) show segments merged incorrectly (order reversed or items combined into the wrong neighbor).
- Root-location bias: open the splitting helper first (functions that call splitlines or re.split), then the merge loop. Look specifically for: collected index lists (merge = []), reversed iteration, and expressions using index+1 or index-1 during concatenation/deletion.
- Why it fails: deleting elements shifts subsequent indices; reversed iteration mitigates some issues but incorrect neighbor selection (using index+1 when the intent was index-1 or vice-versa) or concatenation order (which element is appended to which) produces wrong results.
- Confusable alternatives: incorrect separator set (missing characters in _NON_LINE_BREAKS) or encoding/normalization; rule these out by printing the splitlist before merging.
- Recommended fixes: avoid in-place index arithmetic. Instead scan once and build a new list, merging with the previous element when necessary (e.g., for seg in splitlist: if seg endswith(special): merge into previous else append). Add unit tests for boundary cases including leading/trailing special chars, consecutive special chars, and combinations with CR/LF pairs.
- Evidence preference: failing input strings, the raw list from splitlines(True) before merging, the merge-index collection code, and a minimal patched algorithm showing neighbor-aware merging.

skill.title: api_wrapper_or_sdk_emulator: Response-handler and dispatch priors for SDK emulators
skill.trigger: Failures where client SDK calls (boto3-style) raise KeyError/ClientError or tests assert missing top-level keys (e.g., 'ApplicationResponse'/'ApplicationsResponse') and the repository has modules named responses.py / urls.py / models for services.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: For repositories that implement an SDK emulator (HTTP handlers that mimic a cloud API), the response handler layer (files named responses.py, urls.py) and the central BaseResponse utilities are the primary fault surface for API-contract regressions.
- Prioritize opening service/response handlers (responses.py) and urls.py when SDK calls fail with missing keys or unexpected JSON shapes. Look for: parsing of incoming JSON (are requests expected nested under a wrapper like CreateXRequest?), construction of returned bodies (are returned dicts wrapped under expected envelope keys like 'XResponse' or 'ApplicationsResponse'?), and whether handlers return raw strings vs (status, headers, body) tuples used by central dispatch.
- Check the project's BaseResponse/type dispatch utilities (common file like moto/core/responses.py) to see how handler return values are normalized (_transform_response/_enrich_response) and whether method_dispatch wrappers are used in urls to route HTTP methods correctly.
- Typical localization signals: (1) tests assert presence of a specific envelope key (e.g., 'ApplicationsResponse'), (2) handler code returns a to_json() without wrapping, (3) request parsing reads fields at the wrong nesting level (should look for wrapper keys like 'CreateApplicationRequest'), (4) urls.py uses direct dispatch instead of method_dispatch wrappers which expect specific handler signatures.
Anti_patterns: searching only for backend/model logic (e.g., App.to_json()) without checking the response layer that wraps/unpacks requests and responses. Assuming tests are wrong—first check response handler contract.

Add: In SDK-emulator projects, aggregators that enumerate many service backends (e.g., ResourceGroupsTaggingAPI._get_resources_generator) should prefer stable backend-dict lookups or central accessor helpers (e.g., ec2_backends[account_id][region] or resourcegroupstaggingapi_backends) rather than relying on per-backend alias @property getters which are frequently renamed or removed during refactors; when an AttributeError affects multiple services, prioritize inspecting removed/renamed @property backend getters in the aggregator.

Add: In SDK-emulator projects, also watch for lazy population of in-memory backend model collections (e.g., group.instance_states, backend resource lists). Operations that iterate such collections to apply side effects (protect, tag, deregister) can be no-ops if called before population. Evidence signals: (1) the API method iterates a .instance_states / .instances list to find targets, (2) tests or repro call the mutating API immediately after create without an intervening describe/refresh, (3) model-population helpers exist separately (replace_autoscaling_group_instances, set_desired_capacity, describe_*). Root-location bias: open both the API handler and the model-population code paths; prefer fixes that ensure the mutating operation consults the canonical model accessor or that model population happens deterministically during creation.

Knowledge: Fault mode = missing public attribute initialization/forwarding in wrapper/adapter classes.

- Symptom pattern: immediate AttributeError on attribute access (often at client code or tests), while investigation shows an internal object (e.g., `_active_parser`) that does have the attribute.
- Root-cause bias: look for removed/omitted assignments in __init__ or removed forwarding properties/methods. The wrapper may create the internal object lazily (after __init__), so callers expecting attribute presence fail.

- Confusable alternatives: attribute intentionally removed to make API private (confirm via docs/commits) or attribute now provided by a different accessor; verify by scanning changelog/tests.
- Fix preference: reintroduce explicit initialization (e.g., set self.stack = Stack([...]) or forward to an inner parser via a property) to preserve API compatibility, or document the breaking change and update callers.

- Symptom pattern: immediate AttributeError on attribute access (often at client code or tests), while investigation shows an internal object (e.g., `_active_parser`) that does have the attribute.
- Root-cause bias: look for removed/omitted assignments in __init__ or removed forwarding properties/methods. The wrapper may create the internal object lazily (after __init__), so callers expecting attribute presence fail.
- Evidence signals: constructor does not set the attribute; grep finds usages of `obj.<attr>` across the repo; internal fields like `_active_parser` used later and hold the attribute.
- Confusable alternatives: attribute intentionally removed to make API private (confirm via docs/commits) or attribute now provided by a different accessor; verify by scanning changelog/tests.
- Fix preference: reintroduce explicit initialization (e.g., set self.stack = Stack([...]) or forward to an inner parser via a property) to preserve API compatibility, or document the breaking change and update callers.

Addable sentence: If a class implements attribute delegation (e.g., __getattr__ forwarding to self._stream or similar), prioritize inspecting the wrapper's __init__ for missing assignments or accidental assignment to None; evidence: __getattr__ will raise AttributeError when the delegated field is unset.

edit_history.rationale: The fault is a concrete defect mechanism: a missing public field expected by callers because a wrapper didn't initialize or forward it. Existing fault_mode candidates focused on version-gated missing checks or asymmetric equality; this is a distinct, reusable defect pattern and justifies a new fault_mode skill.

parso/python/diff.py: DiffParser.__init__ does not assign `stack` while _diff_tokenize reads `self._active_parser.stack`.

skill.title: config_merge_prefer_deep_merge_over_dict_union
skill.trigger: Reports where nested configuration properties disappear or are overwritten after aggregating multiple config fragments (e.g., per-file or per-revision definitions); code shows dict union (`|`) or dict.update used in an aggregation loop.
skill.knowledge:
When aggregating configuration fragments that may contain nested dictionaries, shallow merges (dict union `|`, dict.update) are an anti-pattern: they replace whole nested dict values and lose inner keys from earlier fragments. Reusable priors:
- Root-location bias: open the aggregator that folds per-file/per-revision configs before inspecting downstream consumers. The aggregator's merge operator often determines whether nested properties survive.
- Evidence signals: (1) a loop that applies `resolved = resolved | config` or repeated `update()`/`{**a, **b}` in an aggregation, (2) presence elsewhere in the repo of a deep-merge helper (e.g., dpath.merge) indicating the intended semantics, (3) examples/tests demonstrating expected combined nested keys.
- Ranking bias: when a report mentions missing nested config keys, prioritize inspecting merge sites and the exact merge operator/ordering used (including whether configs were reversed) over consumers that read the final config.
- Fix preference: replace shallow merge with a documented recursive/deep-merge helper or ensure an explicit recursive merge that merges nested dicts rather than overwriting them. If order matters, make ordering explicit and document precedence.
- Confusable alternatives: the data source may legitimately provide different nested values (not a merge bug) — confirm that identical inner keys should be combined before changing merge behavior.

edit_history.rationale: This case shows a broadly reusable principle: shallow merges (dict union / update) are an anti-pattern when merging user-supplied config fragments that can contain nested dicts. The lesson is cross-project and does not map cleanly to any existing weak candidate, so create a new general skill to capture the prior.

dvc/repo/plots/__init__.py and other modules use dpath.merge for deep merges elsewhere, showing inconsistent merging choices in the same subsystem.
edit_history.risk: Low — this is a general safety prior. Risk: over-applied advice when overwriting nested dicts is actually intended; recommend confirming intended precedence before changing merge semantics.

skill.title: inspect_config_merge_operators_and_ordering
skill.trigger: Investigation step when aggregated configuration or combined definitions drop nested keys or behave unexpectedly (e.g., only last definition's nested props appear).
skill.knowledge:
Strategy: when nested config properties are missing after aggregation, prioritize the merge site and inspect both operator and order.
Key actions and ranking biases (expressed as durable preferences):
- Preference 1: open the aggregator that folds per-file or per-revision configs (functions named squash/merge/collect) rather than only scanning downstream readers.
- Preference 2: grep for shallow merge idioms (`|`, `.update()`, `{**a, **b}`) inside aggregation loops. If found, treat them as suspicious for nested dict cases.
- Preference 3: grep the repository for deep-merge helpers (dpath.merge, recursive_merge) and compare where/why they are used; inconsistent usage is a clue the aggregator should use the deep helper.
- Preference 4: check iteration order (reversed(configs)) and document precedence; a reversed loop combined with a shallow merge can unintentionally discard earlier nested keys.
- Confusable alternatives: consumer mis-reading keys or intended overwrite behavior — confirm input shapes and expected precedence (tests or docs) before changing merge logic.
- Quick fix ranking: propose replacing shallow merge with the repo's established deep-merge helper and adding a unit test covering nested config combinations.

edit_history.rationale: This trajectory shows a practical, reusable investigation strategy: when nested config properties are lost, inspect the aggregator's merge operator and ordering and compare against deep-merge helpers used elsewhere. No exact existing strategy skill covered this specific 'detect dict union vs deep-merge' hunt, so create a new strategy skill.

skill.title: repo_with_filesystem_abstraction_optional_fs_param: default adapter and early derived-value initialization
skill.trigger: Projects where core classes (Repo/Manager) accept an optional filesystem/adapter parameter (fs=None) and later compute derived variables (root_dir, tmp_dir, join paths) before checking/using them.
skill.knowledge: Project-type prior: In repos that implement a pluggable filesystem/adapter and expose methods with an optional fs parameter, prefer the pattern: (1) apply the canonical default adapter as the first step (e.g., fs = fs or localfs), (2) compute any derived filesystem-dependent locals (e.g., root_dir = fs.abspath(root)) immediately after defaulting, and (3) avoid code paths that reference those derived locals before the default has been applied. Evidence signals: methods that call fs.abspath/fs.join/fs.isdir while accepting fs=None; callers that pass fs=None; diffs/patches that remove or reorder fs-defaulting lines. Ranking bias: when an issue mentions fs=None, raise priority of Repo/Manager modules and their find_root/init helpers over unrelated modules. Confusable alternatives: bugs in the filesystem implementation (LocalFileSystem), or caller misuse intentionally passing None — confirm whether callers normally pass None or an explicit fs instance before changing the callee.

This is a reusable project-level prior distinct from existing 'filesystem_adapter_factory' skills (which focus on class selection by protocol). skill.title: Local variable referenced before assignment due to reordered/late initialization
skill.trigger: Runtime UnboundLocalError naming a local variable (e.g., "local variable 'X' referenced before assignment") inside a function where X is also assigned later or conditionally.
skill.knowledge: Symptom: Python UnboundLocalError that names a local variable usually means that the function both assigns to that name (making it local) and attempts to read it before the assignment executes. Common root cause: the assignment to the local was placed after its first use (for example by moving an assignment below a loop), or the assignment is conditional and not executed on the failing path. Localization lesson: search the failing function for the named variable, find its earliest assignment, and check whether any reads occur earlier. Confusable alternatives: (1) the variable is meant to be global/nonlocal (missing global/nonlocal), (2) name shadowing with a closure—verify scope. Prefer this fault pattern when the variable is assigned inside the same function and an UnboundLocalError names it.
anti_patterns: Assuming the exception always implies an outer-scope missing variable; if the function assigns to the name anywhere, treat it as a local-scope ordering/conditional issue.
Jumping to caller functions without first inspecting the failing function for earlier uses of the named variable.

edit_history.rationale: The ground-truth patch and error clearly illustrate a reusable defect mechanism: a local variable ('bits') was used before its assignment because the assignment was placed after loops that read it. This pattern (UnboundLocalError caused by reassigned/misordered local initialization) is broadly transferable across Python projects and should be captured as a fault-mode skill.

Ground-truth patch: in setup_type_number the original code used 'bits' before it was assigned; fix moves 'bits = util.BCH_type_number(self.version)' above the loop that uses it.
edit_history.risk: Low false-positive rate when the variable is intentionally assigned conditionally in different branches; must still check for global/nonlocal intent and closure shadowing.

skill.knowledge: Strategy: When an UnboundLocalError identifies a variable X, prioritize locating the function(s) where X is assigned and where X is read. skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: argument-validation lives in small SyntaxRule loops over node.children
skill.trigger: Bug reports where many argument-related syntax errors (repeated keyword args, positional after keyword unpacking, unparenthesized generator expression in calls) are no longer reported in a parser library.
skill.knowledge:
In parser/front-end projects, syntactic validation for constructs like function argument lists is commonly implemented inside small SyntaxRule classes (e.g., arglist/argument rules) that iterate node.children and set small state flags (kw_only, kw_unpacking_only, arg_set). Reusable priors:
- When a user reports multiple related argument-validation failures (repeated keyword args, positional-after-keyword, generator-expression parenthesization), prioritize files named errors.py/grammar/rules and classes/registers like @ErrorFinder.register_rule(type='arglist'|'argument').
- Look for loops over node.children (for argument in node.children) and small state flags; these loops implement many localized checks. If many checks are missing, search for removed/short-circuited loop bodies, early returns, or refactors that replaced iteration with a no-op.
- Confusable alternatives: tokenization/AST shape changes (verify node.children contents) and asymmetric equality bugs. Distinguish by printing node.children (types and .value) first; if children look correct but no issues are added, inspect for missing loop bodies or deleted self.add_issue calls.
- Ranking bias: raise priority of opening SyntaxRule implementations and any recent diffs touching them when an entire class of related syntactic checks disappears.

Also watch for PEP8 normalizer implementations (parso/python/pep8.py, PEP8Normalizer._visit_node) where entire rule bodies may have been removed or replaced with a no-op (e.g., a `pass`) during a refactor; these files are high-priority when many style checks vanish. Also check for incorrect membership/substring tests (e.g., `if typ in 'import_name'`) that silently fail to match the intended node types.

Addendum: prioritize opening ErrorFinder/normalizer files for position bugs — check for incorrect indexing of start_pos tuples (using [1] vs [0] unexpectedly) and for places where the message/code/ node args are inserted in the wrong order when storing issues; these mistakes directly change what callers see as line/column or message fields.
anti_patterns: Assuming missing errors imply tokenization is wrong without first opening SyntaxRule implementations.
Only grepping for error messages; miss the structural loop that produces them.

Existing weak parser skills focus on __eq__/child-offset patterns; this is a distinct, actionable pattern (validation implemented by loops over argument nodes that can be accidentally removed). Create a new project_type skill rather than updating an unrelated weak candidate.

- Evidence signals: (1) repro shows the same items appear but in reverse order or mirrored cycles; (2) the generator body contains reversed(), reversed(iterator), list(reversed(...)), slice with [::-1], or loop index arithmetic that runs from len-1 down to 0; (3) diffs showing replacement of 'yield from data' with a manual loop; (4) cycles/length adjustments nearby (off-by-one or cycles += 1) that accompany iteration changes.

- Preferred evidence to confirm: minimal run of the produced generator showing reversed output and a code snippet of the generator body showing reversed()-style iteration. skill.knowledge:
Strategy: inspect_syntax_rules_and_node_children_loops — When a parser accepts invalid constructs across multiple examples, use these steps as high-priority checks:
1) Grep for rule registrations and likely message text (e.g., `register_rule(type='arglist'|'argument')`, 'keyword argument repeated', 'positional argument follows').
2) Open the corresponding rule implementations and search for iteration over node.children (e.g., `for argument in node.children:`) and small state flags (kw_only, kw_unpacking_only, arg_set). These loops often implement many related checks.
3) Print or inspect node.children (types and .value) for representative inputs to distinguish AST-shape issues from missing validation logic.
4) Inspect recent diffs for deletions or early returns that would prevent the loop body from running; if the loop or its self.add_issue calls were removed, many checks will vanish.
Ranking preference: raise priority of opening the rule implementation and recent diffs touching it when multiple related syntactic checks disappear.

When opening the registered rule (e.g., PEP8Normalizer._visit_node) add these checks: (1) look for bodies replaced by no-ops (`pass`) or early returns/continues that prevent self.add_issue calls; (2) search for incorrect conditional patterns (e.g., `if typ in 'import_name'` using substring membership) that will silently fail to match intended node types; (3) prefer comparing recent diffs of the rule file before assuming AST changes.
anti_patterns: Stopping at top-level callers and patching downstream behavior without opening the rule implementation.
Assuming AST-shape is wrong before checking whether validation code was removed or disabled.

skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: wrapper/parser classes must preserve Parser public attributes (stack) or initialize equivalents
skill.trigger: Reports of AttributeError when reading attributes on a parser-like wrapper (e.g., `DiffParser.stack`) or behavior changes where code external to the wrapper expects attributes that the core Parser exposes.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: Libraries that implement a thin wrapper or alternate parser (incremental/diff parser, compatibility adapter) should preserve the public attribute surface of the original Parser, or explicitly initialize/forward commonly-consumed attributes (notably `stack`).

- Observable signals: AttributeError on accessing attribute (e.g., `obj.stack`); code contains an internal parser like `_active_parser` that has the attribute; constructor (__init__) does not assign the attribute.
- Root-location bias: inspect the wrapper class __init__ first, then search for internal fields (e.g., `_active_parser`) and how they are created. Compare with the canonical Parser class to find missing assignments.
- Confusable alternatives: the attribute could have been intentionally removed (check changelog/commit message) or made private; confirm by searching for uses across the repo and tests that assume it exists.
- Ranking bias: raise the priority of checks that confirm public API compatibility (constructor assignments or explicit forwarding methods) when a user-visible AttributeError is reported in parser-like modules.

edit_history.rationale: Existing parser-oriented candidate skills focus on node equality and child indexing, not on wrapper/adapter compatibility of public Parser attributes. This case clearly shows a reusable project-type pattern: parser wrappers must preserve Parser's public surface (or initialize equivalent attributes). Creating a new project_type skill keeps the lesson focused and avoids diluting the existing parser equality skill.

skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: Node/Leaf equality and child-offset patterns
skill.trigger: Bug reports about AST/parameter/token parsing that show incorrect booleans for token presence or IndexError when accessing child tokens.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: In parser/front-end libraries, token node types often implement custom equality (e.g., comparing a Leaf to a string by returning self.value == other). This design makes direct equality with strings readable but creates brittle interactions with language-level operations that invoke equality on the other operand (for example tuple membership checks use element == candidate, so a membership test like `node in ('*','**')` will call str.__eq__ and not node.__eq__). Additionally, parser code commonly uses integer offsets into children lists to skip optional tokens (annotations, star markers, commas). Reusable priors:
- Prioritize files/classes named tree.py, node.py, parser/, and classes called Param/Tfpdef/Leaf when parsing/parameter bugs appear.
- Inspect __eq__ / comparison helpers and any code that computes offsets with expressions like `int(self.children[0] in ('*','**'))` or `children[offset]`.
- Expect two confusable code paths: (1) wrong offset (child index off-by-one) causing incorrect default/annotation/star detection; (2) asymmetric equality causing membership/comparison to behave invertedly. Both can coexist.
- When verifying fixes prefer explicit comparisons (e.g., check .value or compare types) or compute offsets using integer checks based on token values using the same side of equality (e.g., compare child.value in set) to avoid relying on reversed __eq__ semantics.
Anti_patterns: assume Node vs str comparisons are symmetric; ignore small helper mixins that override __eq__ and affect membership checks.
anti_patterns: Assuming membership checks (x in ('a','b')) behave the same when x is a custom node type that defines __eq__; they can be asymmetric.

skill.title: boundary_inclusive_exclusive_miscalculation_in_position_search
skill.trigger: ValueError/lookup failure for positions that lie exactly on element boundaries (start_pos or end_pos) in position-based searches; binary-search or range-selection code present.
skill.knowledge:
Fault-mode knowledge: When code locates an element by position using a binary search or range comparisons over child start_pos/end_pos, bugs often arise from incorrect inclusive/exclusive comparisons or from mid-index rounding biases.
- Observable signals: (1) a ValueError or lookup-failure reported for positions that equal a child's start or end, (2) binary_search-like code that computes an index and compares position <= element.end_pos or position < element.start_pos, (3) pre-checks that hard-code lower/upper bounds (e.g., (1, 0)).
- Root-location bias: inspect the position-lookup implementation (get_leaf_for_position, get_node_at_pos, index-of-position helpers) and any binary-search helper; check both the pre-boundary guard and the recursive/iterative partition logic that uses <= vs < and how the mid index is computed (floor vs ceil).
- Confusable alternatives: genuine tokenizer/tree construction problems (verify by printing children start_pos/end_pos for the failing input). Distinguish by reproducing the lookup on the parsed tree and stepping the binary search.
- Fix preference: make inclusive/exclusive choices explicit and symmetric (decide whether child.start_pos belongs to the earlier or later interval and apply consistently), ensure pre-check range tests match the binary-search assumptions, and use mid-index rounding that matches recursion endpoints (round-up vs round-down) so recursion base cases correctly select the intended child. skill.knowledge:
Strategy: When a reported AttributeError names a missing method, prefer an evidence-driven search-and-trace that prioritizes refactor/move/deletion causes:
- Search order & ranking bias:
  1) Open the reported class definition to confirm whether the method currently exists.
  2) Grep repo for the exact method name (e.g., 'def write(') and for 'ClassName' occurrences; if matches are missing or sparse, raise likelihood of deletion/move.
  3) Grep likely container modules (util.py, data.py, core.py, helpers/). Small libraries often place core methods in utility modules that may have been refactored.
  4) If greps fail, inspect packaging layout (is the package split across modules?) and tests/examples that call the method — these show intended public surface.
  5) If available, consult VCS history / changelog / commit messages for refactors or method removals. If history indicates a move, search for the method name in older revisions or alternate module names.

- Fix preference: where backward compatibility matters, prefer adding a small forwarding shim or reintroducing a method at the original public API location rather than modifying many callers.
- Confusable alternatives: wrong-instance type, packaging/import-time issues, or missing initialization — always confirm object.__class__ and constructor logic before assuming deletion.

skill.trigger: Reports where stream or frame-producing generators yield the wrong number of items, drop frames, or produce truncated/shifted sequences after a refactor or logic change.
skill.knowledge:
Fault-mode: incorrect pairing of finite iterators (range/limited index lists) with infinite or long-lived generators often miscomputes which elements are yielded and how many. Observable signals:
- A generator/producer function uses zip(range(...), generator) or pairs a finite index sequence with an infinite producer and then applies an if/conditional to gate yields.
- Symptoms: produced sequences are shorter/longer than expected, frames are missing or shifted, many variants that rely on the same producer all show incorrect outputs.

Root-location bias: open the frame/stream producer (functions named *_frames, frame_data, _generator, compile/assemble helpers) and inspect loop constructs that combine ranges and other iterators. Look for: zip(range(...), gen), zip(some_index_list, gen), conditional yield guards using i<=size, and any places where an index list is computed separately from the producer.

Why it fails: zip(range(n), gen) stops after n pairs but may not align with the intended bound or may be masked by additional conditionals; conversely enumerating the generator and using an explicit break at the desired size reliably bounds consumption. Off-by-one checks (<= vs >=) and inverted polarity further confuse yield counts.

Confusable alternatives: an algorithmic bug inside transformation logic that changes frame contents — rule this out by instrumenting the raw producer yields (print/collect the first N items directly) before downstream formatting.

Fix preference: prefer enumerating the (possibly infinite) producer and apply a clear break condition (for i, item in enumerate(gen): if i >= bound: break; yield item) or build a finite slice via itertools.islice(gen, bound). Make boundary checks explicit and write unit tests that assert exact produced sequence lengths and sample outputs for small sizes.

skill.title: inspect_syntax_rules_and_node_children_loops
skill.trigger: Parser accepts many invalid inputs of the same family (e.g., argument-list syntax issues); grep finds rule registrations or message strings but user-observed errors are not produced.
skill.knowledge:
Strategy: inspect_syntax_rules_and_node_children_loops — When a parser accepts invalid constructs across multiple examples, use these steps as high-priority checks:
1) Grep for rule registrations and likely message text (e.g., `register_rule(type='arglist'|'argument')`, 'keyword argument repeated', 'positional argument follows').
2) Open the corresponding rule implementations and search for iteration over node.children (e.g., `for argument in node.children:`) and small state flags (kw_only, kw_unpacking_only, arg_set). These loops often implement many related checks.
3) Print or inspect node.children (types and .value) for representative inputs to distinguish AST-shape issues from missing validation logic.
4) Inspect recent diffs for deletions or early returns that would prevent the loop body from running; if the loop or its self.add_issue calls were removed, many checks will vanish.
Ranking preference: raise priority of opening the rule implementation and recent diffs touching it when multiple related syntactic checks disappear.

When opening the registered rule (e.g., PEP8Normalizer._visit_node) add these checks: (1) look for bodies replaced by no-ops (`pass`) or early returns/continues that prevent self.add_issue calls; (2) search for incorrect conditional patterns (e.g., `if typ in 'import_name'` using substring membership) that will silently fail to match intended node types; (3) prefer comparing recent diffs of the rule file before assuming AST changes.
anti_patterns: Stopping at top-level callers and patching downstream behavior without opening the rule implementation.
Assuming AST-shape is wrong before checking whether validation code was removed or disabled.

This is a reusable strategy distinct from existing 'inspect_custom_eq_and_child_indexing' and merits a dedicated strategy skill.

skill.title: api_wrapper_or_sdk_emulator: Response-handler and dispatch priors for SDK emulators
skill.trigger: Failures where client SDK calls (boto3-style) raise KeyError/ClientError or tests assert missing top-level keys (e.g., 'ApplicationResponse'/'ApplicationsResponse') and the repository has modules named responses.py / urls.py / models for services.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: For repositories that implement an SDK emulator (HTTP handlers that mimic a cloud API), the response handler layer (files named responses.py, urls.py) and the central BaseResponse utilities are the primary fault surface for API-contract regressions.
- Prioritize opening service/response handlers (responses.py) and urls.py when SDK calls fail with missing keys or unexpected JSON shapes. Look for: parsing of incoming JSON (are requests expected nested under a wrapper like CreateXRequest?), construction of returned bodies (are returned dicts wrapped under expected envelope keys like 'XResponse' or 'ApplicationsResponse'?), and whether handlers return raw strings vs (status, headers, body) tuples used by central dispatch.
- Check the project's BaseResponse/type dispatch utilities (common file like moto/core/responses.py) to see how handler return values are normalized (_transform_response/_enrich_response) and whether method_dispatch wrappers are used in urls to route HTTP methods correctly.
- Typical localization signals: (1) tests assert presence of a specific envelope key (e.g., 'ApplicationsResponse'), (2) handler code returns a to_json() without wrapping, (3) request parsing reads fields at the wrong nesting level (should look for wrapper keys like 'CreateApplicationRequest'), (4) urls.py uses direct dispatch instead of method_dispatch wrappers which expect specific handler signatures.
Anti_patterns: searching only for backend/model logic (e.g., App.to_json()) without checking the response layer that wraps/unpacks requests and responses. Assuming tests are wrong—first check response handler contract.

Add: In SDK-emulator projects, aggregators that enumerate many service backends (e.g., ResourceGroupsTaggingAPI._get_resources_generator) should prefer stable backend-dict lookups or central accessor helpers (e.g., ec2_backends[account_id][region] or resourcegroupstaggingapi_backends) rather than relying on per-backend alias @property getters which are frequently renamed or removed during refactors; when an AttributeError affects multiple services, prioritize inspecting removed/renamed @property backend getters in the aggregator.

Add: In SDK-emulator projects, also watch for lazy population of in-memory backend model collections (e.g., group.instance_states, backend resource lists). Operations that iterate such collections to apply side effects (protect, tag, deregister) can be no-ops if called before population. Evidence signals: (1) the API method iterates a .instance_states / .instances list to find targets, (2) tests or repro call the mutating API immediately after create without an intervening describe/refresh, (3) model-population helpers exist separately (replace_autoscaling_group_instances, set_desired_capacity, describe_*). Root-location bias: open both the API handler and the model-population code paths; prefer fixes that ensure the mutating operation consults the canonical model accessor or that model population happens deterministically during creation.

Add: In SDK-emulator services, check for creator/serializer key-name and initialization mismatches: creators may map incoming envelope keys (e.g., 'OnUpload'/'OnPartialUpload') into internal keys (e.g., 'on_upload'/'on_partial_upload'); serializers (to_dict/response builders) must use the same internal keys and initialize any lists/dicts they append to before use. Missing initialization or inconsistent key casing is a recurrent source of missing fields or NameError-like failures in describe/serialize flows.

edit_history.rationale: This case reveals a reusable repository-family prior: SDK/emulator projects (like moto) centralize HTTP-to-backend translation in response handler modules and urls dispatch. Creating a project_type skill captures where to look (responses.py, urls.py, models backends, and central BaseResponse helpers) for similar failures across other services.

skill.title: incorrect_generator_iteration_and_boundary_with_infinite_producer_causing_frame_loss
skill.trigger: Reports where stream or frame-producing generators yield the wrong number of items, drop frames, or produce truncated/shifted sequences after a refactor or logic change.
skill.knowledge:
Fault-mode: incorrect pairing of finite iterators (range/limited index lists) with infinite or long-lived generators often miscomputes which elements are yielded and how many. Observable signals:
- A generator/producer function uses zip(range(...), generator) or pairs a finite index sequence with an infinite producer and then applies an if/conditional to gate yields.
- Symptoms: produced sequences are shorter/longer than expected, frames are missing or shifted, many variants that rely on the same producer all show incorrect outputs.

Root-location bias: open the frame/stream producer (functions named *_frames, frame_data, _generator, compile/assemble helpers) and inspect loop constructs that combine ranges and other iterators. Look for: zip(range(...), gen), zip(some_index_list, gen), conditional yield guards using i<=size, and any places where an index list is computed separately from the producer.

Why it fails: zip(range(n), gen) stops after n pairs but may not align with the intended bound or may be masked by additional conditionals; conversely enumerating the generator and using an explicit break at the desired size reliably bounds consumption. Off-by-one checks (<= vs >=) and inverted polarity further confuse yield counts.

Confusable alternatives: an algorithmic bug inside transformation logic that changes frame contents — rule this out by instrumenting the raw producer yields (print/collect the first N items directly) before downstream formatting.

Fix preference: prefer enumerating the (possibly infinite) producer and apply a clear break condition (for i, item in enumerate(gen): if i >= bound: break; yield item) or build a finite slice via itertools.islice(gen, bound). Make boundary checks explicit and write unit tests that assert exact produced sequence lengths and sample outputs for small sizes.

edit_history.rationale: The ground-truth patch shows a clear, reusable defect mechanism: replacing zip(range(...), infinite_generator)+conditional-yield with enumerate(infinite_generator)+explicit break. This is a transferable fault-mode (applies to streaming/animation producers, compiler-like generator assemblers, and other infinite-producer consumers) and is not identical to any single weak candidate in the provided slot, so create a focused new fault_mode skill.

skill.title: parser_or_compiler_frontend: tree/leaf string-field initialization and propagation (prefix) must be explicit
skill.trigger: TypeError or NoneType errors during parsing originating from string operations (concatenation or slicing) involving node/leaf prefix fields or other small string metadata.
skill.knowledge:
Knowledge: In parser/front-end projects, small string metadata on leaf/node objects (commonly named prefix, value, or similar) are propagated and aggregated by specialized tree-manipulation routines (copy_nodes, _remove_endmarker, finish/close). These fields must have explicit, safe defaults (typically empty string) in constructors. Observable signals: TypeError mentioning 'NoneType' and string operations, code locations that read or concatenate `.prefix` (e.g., prefix + first_leaf.prefix or last_leaf.prefix[:n]). Root-location bias: open tree/node class __init__ and the tree construction code (e.g., _NodesTree.__init__), then inspect the copy/merge helpers that assign from leaves (copy_nodes, _remove_endmarker, finish). Confusable alternatives: tokenizer returning unexpected None prefixes (check token construction), or intentional API change that makes prefix optional (confirm via changelog/tests). Ranking bias: raise priority of files named tree.py/diff.py and methods that copy/assign prefix when string-operation TypeErrors occur in parsing modules.

Add: Also prioritize multi-value-returning helper routines (e.g., copy_nodes/_copy_nodes) and call sites where their tuple return values are unpacked directly into parser internal state (for example: new_nodes, self._working_stack, self.prefix, added_indents = ...). Observable signal: callers that immediately assign into core fields (self._working_stack/self.prefix) and later crash with AttributeError when those fields are used. When present, inspect both the helper's return statements (ordering, early/conditional returns) and the callers' unpacking to verify types and ordering remain stable.

skill.title: refactor_inverted_condition_early_return_in_traversal
skill.trigger: Regression where ancestor/traversal helpers suddenly return None or the original node instead of an ancestor after a refactor; diffs show inverted conditions or moved returns inside loops.
skill.knowledge: Fault-mode: small traversal/refactor inversion causing early return. Knowledge: Many codebases implement parent-walking or boundary-search routines as simple loops: `node = node.parent; while node is not None: if node.type in TYPES: return node; node = node.parent; return None`. A common regression after refactor is an inverted condition or misplaced return (for example `if node.type not in TYPES: return None` inside the loop, or returning the original input at the end). Observable signals: (1) tests that previously found an ancestor now get None or the same node, (2) diffs that change the membership test polarity or move/replace return statements inside the loop, (3) multiple, near-identical implementations in the repo (module-level helper and instance-method) that have diverged. Root-location bias: open the traversal function(s) implementing parent-walking loops first and compare against tests. Also parity-check other implementations of the same logic (module-level vs method-level vs similar helper in other modules). Confusable alternatives: asymmetric equality or token-type changes (verify node.type and child layouts); incorrect helper returns from nested helpers that feed the traversal (verify helpers' final return values). Ranking bias: when ancestor-search symptom is reported, prioritize recent diffs to traversal loops and compare parallel implementations and unit tests that assert identity of returned ancestor.

edit_history.rationale: This case demonstrates a distinct, reusable defect mode: small parent-walking or traversal loops whose conditional logic was inverted or whose return was misplaced during a refactor, causing early exit or wrong final return. Existing fault weak candidates focus on child-indexing or asymmetric equality; they do not capture the specific refactor/inverted-condition early-return pattern. Creating a new fault-mode skill keeps the lesson focused and reusable.

skill.title: compare_parallel_parent_walking_implementations_and_check_loop_returns
skill.trigger: Reports that ancestor/position search or other tree traversal functions return wrong values (None or original node) unexpectedly, especially when multiple similar helpers exist in the codebase.
skill.knowledge: Strategy: 1) Reproduce the symptom with a minimal input that previously passed (small parse producing the expected ancestor). 2) Open the failing traversal helper and identify the loop and its membership test(s). Check if the membership condition was inverted or if a return was added inside the loop that returns on 'not-match'. 3) Locate parallel implementations (same function name in module and methods on Node classes, or similar helpers in other modules) and do a side-by-side comparison: ensure the membership test, return-on-match branch, and final return are consistent. 4) If divergence is found, inspect recent diffs for the file(s) and prioritize fixes that restore the original 'return-on-match / final None' behavior; prefer unit tests that assert ancestor identity. Ranking bias: when ancestor-search symptoms appear, rank small traversal helpers and recent diffs above deeper callers; prefer parity checks across implementations early in the investigation. Confusable alternatives: membership/equality asymmetry or tokenization changes — confirm by printing node.type and values before changing loop logic.
